opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really natural question, because there's an enormous amount of compute that's already been sunk into autoregressive models, and it would be wasteful to just throw all of that away and start from scratch every time you want to try a different generative paradigm.

The way I think about it is that a lot of what a pretrained autoregressive model has learned isn't really specific to left-to-right generation. It's learned representations of language, facts about the world, syntax, some reasoning ability. All of that lives in the weights, and in principle it should transfer. The ordering, the causal mask, is in some sense just one particular way of factorizing the distribution. So the hope is that you can take those weights as an initialization and then adapt the model to a different objective, in our case a discrete diffusion or denoising objective, where the model learns to predict many tokens in parallel and iteratively refine a sequence rather than committing to one token at a time.

In practice there are some things you have to be careful about. The architecture has to change a bit: you typically move from a causal attention mask to bidirectional attention, because in diffusion every position can condition on every other position. And there's a distribution shift. The autoregressive model has only ever seen clean prefixes, whereas a diffusion model has to deal with partially masked or noisy inputs at many different noise levels. So you need a continued training phase, sometimes with an annealing schedule where you gradually relax the causal structure, so that you don't destroy what the model already knows.

What's encouraging is that the adaptation is much cheaper than pretraining from scratch. You can get to a diffusion model that's competitive with similarly sized autoregressive models using a fraction of the tokens. And then you get the benefits that motivate diffusion in the first place: parallel generation, so much faster inference, the ability to do infilling and editing naturally, and more flexible control over the output.

I'd also say it's a bit of a pragmatic bridge. Long term, I think there are good reasons to believe diffusion-style models trained natively could be very competitive. But right now, leveraging the existing autoregressive ecosystem is the fastest way to show what these models can do at scale, and to get them into people's hands.

r001.rationale: It identifies changing from causal to bidirectional attention as a key adaptation, since diffusion positions condition on one another.

r002.rationale: It mentions bidirectional attention and diffusion benefits, but does not attribute a quality advantage to using context on both sides when deciding what to change.

r003.rationale: It describes an annealing schedule that gradually relaxes the causal structure.

r004.rationale: It does not describe converting autoregressive likelihood into a score function.

r005.rationale: It does not describe training on synthetic samples generated by an autoregressive model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something we've thought about a lot, because the honest reality is that the big autoregressive models represent an enormous investment of compute, and it would be a shame to throw that away and start from scratch just because you want a different generative paradigm.

The key insight is that at the architecture level, an autoregressive transformer and a diffusion language model are actually very similar. In both cases you have a transformer that takes in a sequence of tokens and outputs a distribution over tokens at each position. The real differences are twofold. One is the attention mask: an autoregressive model uses a causal mask, so each position only sees what came before it, while a diffusion model uses bidirectional attention, because when you're denoising a sequence you want every position to see the full context on both sides. The second is the training objective: next-token prediction versus what's essentially a masked prediction objective, where you corrupt some fraction of the tokens and ask the model to recover them, with that fraction varying across noise levels.

So the natural recipe is to take the pretrained weights, drop the causal mask, and continue training with the diffusion objective. And what you find is that a surprisingly large amount of the knowledge transfers. The model already knows the statistics of language, it already knows facts about the world, it already has good token representations. What it needs to learn is how to use bidirectional context and how to handle inputs where a large fraction of the tokens are masked, which is a very different input distribution from what it saw during pretraining. That adaptation turns out to be much cheaper than pretraining from scratch, often by one or two orders of magnitude in terms of tokens.

There are a few subtleties. If you flip the attention mask all at once, there's an initial shock to the model, and you can lose some capabilities temporarily. So one thing that helps is to do the transition more gradually, for example annealing from causal to bidirectional attention, or mixing the two objectives for a while. Another is that the masking schedule matters: autoregressive models are implicitly very good at the regime where almost everything is unmasked and you're predicting one token, so you want the diffusion training to spend more of its effort on the heavily masked regimes the base model has never seen.

And then there's a nice conceptual point, which is that autoregressive generation is really a special case of this framework. Generating left to right is one particular unmasking order. Diffusion lets you choose any order, or unmask many tokens in parallel, which is where you get the speed advantages. So reusing the autoregressive model isn't a hack; you're starting from a point that's already inside the space of models you care about and expanding what it can do.

I'll say the thing I find most exciting is what this means practically. It means the question of autoregressive versus diffusion doesn't have to be a bet you make before you spend tens of millions of dollars on pretraining. You can make that investment once and then adapt. That lowers the barrier for the whole community to explore this direction, and I think we'll see a lot of progress as a result.

r002.rationale: It explains that bidirectional context helps denoising, but does not attribute a potential quality advantage over autoregressive models to that ability.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the transition can be made gradually by annealing from causal to bidirectional attention.

r005.rationale: It does not describe using autoregressive-generated samples as synthetic training data.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a way to reuse the investment we’ve already made in training autoregressive models. Those models have learned a tremendous amount about language, so the question is: can we transfer that knowledge to a model with a different generation process, instead of learning everything again from scratch?

An autoregressive model predicts the next token given a prefix. A diffusion language model learns to recover tokens from a corrupted sequence—for example, a sequence where some tokens have been masked out. So you can initialize with the pretrained weights, then continue training with a denoising objective. Depending on the architecture, that can also involve changing the attention mask so the model can use context on both sides of a missing token.

The weights give you a useful starting point, but there’s still an adaptation problem. The model has to learn to make predictions under these different patterns of missing information. The interesting questions are how much additional training that takes, how much of the original capability you retain, and whether you get useful benefits from being able to generate multiple tokens in parallel or revise a sequence over several steps.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts prefix-only autoregressive prediction with using context on both sides, and identifies changing the attention mask and adapting to missing-information patterns as part of the challenge.

r002.rationale: It mentions access to context on both sides but does not attribute a potential quality advantage to that ability when deciding what to change.

r003.rationale: It mentions changing the attention mask, but does not describe gradually annealing it from causal to noncausal.

r004.rationale: It does not describe converting an autoregressive likelihood into a diffusion score function.

r005.rationale: It does not describe training the diffusion model on synthetic samples generated by an autoregressive model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very natural direction, because training a language model from scratch is extremely expensive. We already have autoregressive models that have learned a tremendous amount about language, so the question is whether we can reuse that knowledge while changing the way we generate text.

An autoregressive model is trained to predict the next token given the preceding tokens. A diffusion model has a different task: it needs to recover text from a corrupted version, potentially using context on both sides. So you can use the pretrained model as an initialization, but you still need to adapt it to that denoising objective. It’s not simply a matter of changing the sampler.

The interesting question is how much additional training you need, and how much of the original model’s capability you can preserve. If that adaptation is efficient, then you have a way to take advantage of the investment in autoregressive models while exploring generation that can update multiple tokens in parallel and revise earlier decisions.
